title: Could You Survive Inside a Hurricane?
credits: Footage: NASA (ISS crew photography, Space Shuttle photography, JPL/MISR/AIRS imagery, Kennedy Space Center and Stennis damage surveys, GRIP and Global Hawk photography; public domain). Facts: NOAA National Hurricane Center, NASA.

scenes.text: This is the eye of a hurricane. Could you survive standing inside it?
scenes.yt_chapter: Could you survive inside a hurricane?

scenes.text: A Category 4 hurricane is coming for your coast. Stay until the end, and I will show you what really kills people. It is not the wind.
label: HURRICANE
Could you survive it?

scenes.text: A hurricane is a giant heat engine. Warm ocean water, above about twenty-six degrees Celsius, feeds it moisture. Rising air spins as Earth rotates, and the storm organizes into a rotating wall of thunderstorms hundreds of kilometers wide.
label: TROPICAL CYCLONE
Fuelled by warm water
scenes.fact: Same storm: hurricane in the Atlantic,\Ntyphoon in the northwest Pacific.

scenes.caption: WIND SPEED WHERE A STORM BECOMES A HURRICANE
scenes.text: At seventy-four miles per hour, or one hundred nineteen kilometers per hour, a tropical storm earns the name hurricane.

scenes.heading: THE SAFFIR-SIMPSON SCALE
scenes.text: The Saffir-Simpson scale rates hurricanes from one to five. Category five means sustained winds above two hundred fifty-two kilometers per hour. Category four, your storm, starts at two hundred nine.
Now you reach the center. First comes the eyewall, a ring of the fiercest thunderstorms, with the strongest winds of the whole storm. Trees snap, roofs peel away, and debris flies like missiles.
scenes.yt_chapter: What is inside the eye of a hurricane?
label: THE EYEWALL
Strongest winds

scenes.text: Then, suddenly, it stops. In the eye the wind drops, the clouds part, and you may see blue sky, or even stars. It feels like the storm is over.
label: THE EYE
Calm, for a while
scenes.fact: Eyes are often tens of km wide, so the\Ncalm can pass in under an hour.

scenes.text: As the eye moves on, the opposite eyewall arrives, and the wind returns from the opposite direction. People who step outside in the eye can be caught in the open.

scenes.question: What causes the most deaths in hurricanes?
scenes.text: Quick test. What causes the most deaths in hurricanes?

Water. Storm surge is a dome of seawater pushed ashore by the winds, and it is the deadliest part of a hurricane. In 2005, surge and flooding from Katrina swamped much of the Gulf Coast, including most of New Orleans.
scenes.yt_chapter: What kills the most people in a hurricane?
label: STORM SURGE
The deadliest part

scenes.caption: OF MOVING WATER CAN FLOAT MANY CARS
scenes.text: Just thirty centimeters of moving water can float many cars.
Rain adds a second flood. In 2017, Hurricane Harvey stalled over Texas and dropped more than a meter of rain in places, flooding huge areas for days.
label: HURRICANE HARVEY
scenes.fact: A slow hurricane can be as deadly as a\Nstrong one: the rain keeps falling.

scenes.text: So can you survive? Scientists do fly into and above these storms, with aircraft like NASA's DC-8 and Global Hawk, and their data improves forecasts. But they are trained, and they leave.
label: NASA RESEARCH
Flying into storms

scenes.text: The real answer is to leave. Surge can destroy buildings, and a roof is no shelter from the sea. Evacuate when told, and go inland and uphill. Forecasts now give days of warning, which has saved countless lives.
label: THE REAL ANSWER
Leave early

scenes.text: Would you stay, or go? Tell me in the comments. Subscribe to Oddly Logical Science for more stories where science meets survival.

Could you survive inside a hurricane? Follow a Category 4 storm to its eye and learn what really kills people: not the wind, but the water.

In this video:
- How does a hurricane form?
- What is inside the eye?
- What actually kills people in a hurricane?
- Could you survive?

FAQ
What is a hurricane? A tropical cyclone with sustained winds of at least 119 km/h (74 mph).
Is the eye calm? Yes, for a while, but the opposite eyewall follows.
What is the deadliest part? Water: storm surge and rain flooding.
